channel_name: Invest Like the Best · Patrick O'Shaughnessy
video_title: Why OpenAI and Anthropic Won't Win Finance
gist: Rogo CEO Gabe argues that within 10 years the majority of enterprise value at top investment firms and banks will sit in software/data systems rather than people, and that Rogo can win finance not by out-modeling OpenAI/Anthropic but by building the compliance, data-room, and transaction-plumbing layer the labs will never bother with.

themes.theme: AI Disruption Timeline for Investment Firms

insights.claim: Rogo's CEO predicts that in 10 years the world's best investment firms and banks will hold 90% of their enterprise value in software, data, and systems rather than in people, versus roughly 90% in people today.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Investors should watch which incumbent firms are actively converting proprietary human judgment into owned software/data assets now, since that ratio may become a leading indicator of which franchises survive.
insights.quote: In 10 years, the world's best investment firms, best banks will be have 90% of their enterprise value, not in people, but in software and data and systems.

insights.claim: The actionable question for any investment firm leader today is how to extract what lives in the 'latent minds' of the best people and encode it into a system the firm owns and operates, rather than letting that knowledge walk out the door with employees.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete due-diligence question for evaluating incumbent financial firms: ask what percentage of top-performer knowledge has been systematized versus still trapped in individual heads.

insights.claim: Jane Street took roughly 15 years to build its dominant technology-driven franchise in market making and quant trading, and Rogo's CEO expects the best investors today have only 2-5 years to figure out how to integrate AI into their own workflows before a similar competitive gap opens up.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Sets a rough time window (2-5 years) for handicapping which incumbent asset managers and banks successfully reinvent themselves versus lose share to AI-native entrants.

insights.claim: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's framing that every organization is heading toward having 'a data center full of geniuses' is cited by Rogo's CEO as the reason incumbent banks and funds (Goldman, Millennium, Citadel) will need years to figure out how to restructure their businesses even after gaining access to vastly more raw intelligence.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO), citing Dario Amodei
insights.so_what: Raw model intelligence alone won't reorganize a firm's org chart or workflows automatically — organizational redesign lags capability, creating a window for AI-native challengers.
insights.quote: everyone's going to have a data center full of geniuses or a country full of geniuses

insights.claim: For the first time in decades, private equity firms, hedge funds, and investment banks face a genuine innovator's-dilemma-style threat, because their historically stable, fund-raising-driven business models had structural momentum that had insulated them from disruption until AI-native competitors emerged.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Legacy financial-services incumbents that assume their franchise momentum (fund-to-fund raising, brand) protects them from AI disruption may be structurally exposed for the first time in a generation.
insights.quote: there has not been an innovator's dilemma for private equity firms, for hedge funds, for investment banks in a long time.

insights.claim: There are roughly 300,000 American businesses too small to know what Goldman Sachs does and too small for JPMorgan to service profitably; Rogo's CEO argues AI-driven cost reduction in dealmaking could extend capital-markets access to this underserved long tail, echoing how greater market liquidity has historically had large positive economic effects over the ~300-400 year history of modern capital markets.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A large underserved SMB capital-formation market becomes addressable if AI collapses the cost of dealmaking — a potential new TAM for banks and fintech that can serve it profitably.
insights.quote: the 300,000 American businesses that couldn't even tell you what Goldman Sachs does and JP Morgan doesn't have the time to go out and work with them because the business is too small.

themes.theme: Rogo's Product Evolution & Model Capability Jumps

insights.claim: Rogo's product went from unreliable to genuinely useful in two distinct model-driven eras: OpenAI's o1-Pro was the first model reliable enough to act as a decent financial search/calculation tool, and Anthropic's Opus 4.5 (released around the end of 2025/beginning of 2026) made models capable of doing essentially anything a junior investment banking or investing analyst does, given the right instructions and context.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete capability timeline investors can use to date when 'junior analyst-level' automation became real in finance, useful for benchmarking other vertical AI products against the same model generations.

insights.claim: Applied AI companies that built ahead of model capability suffered a 'first-mover disadvantage' — early demos looked magical but the product was unreliable, so prospects tried it, called it garbage, and moved on; once the underlying models caught up, the same architecture became magical rather than getting credit for being early.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: When evaluating an early-stage vertical AI startup that looks unimpressive today, check whether the team is building correctly for a future model generation rather than assuming current output quality reflects the ceiling.

insights.claim: Cognition's own marketing now jokes about its AI coding agent Devin's early bad reputation ('remember Devin? It's good now'), illustrating a broader pattern where applied-AI products launched ahead of model capability first look like failures before later becoming genuinely excellent.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A recurring pattern (bad launch reputation -> later vindication) to watch for when assessing whether an early agentic product's poor initial reviews are a red flag or just premature timing.
insights.quote: cognition is very famous for like literally their ads now say remember Devon like it's good now.

insights.claim: Rogo built a workflow letting a bank managing director simply email a markup of a deck to Rogo's AI analyst instead of a human analyst, returning the markup in about 20 minutes versus roughly 2 days, while automatically alerting and giving full audit visibility to the human junior analyst on the deal.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete example (~2 days to 20 minutes) of the magnitude of time compression achievable in investment banking deal workflows, useful for sizing productivity claims from finance AI vendors.
insights.quote: We make it so easy for a managing director at a bank to email a markup of a deck...to our AI analyst over email, and then returning that markup in 20 minutes as opposed to 2 days.

insights.claim: Investors are willing to pay roughly $50,000 for a single high-quality investment idea, which is why multi-agent products that run thousands of agents debating for 24 hours to surface one final recommendation are economically viable in finance in a way that would not work in most other domains.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Finance's willingness to pay large sums for a single insight justifies token-intensive multi-agent architectures that would be uneconomical elsewhere — a structural advantage for finance-focused AI products over consumer or generic verticals.
insights.quote: investors are happy to pay $50,000 for one really good idea

insights.claim: A bank managing director who hadn't personally opened an Excel file in roughly 20 years reported creating a 5-page client deliverable himself in 10 minutes using Rogo, a task that previously required 3 days of back-and-forth with a human analyst.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Illustrates that AI adoption in banking is reaching even senior, non-technical dealmakers, not just junior analysts — a signal that productivity gains are broad-based, though not yet translating into firm-level metrics (see pricing/adoption theme).
insights.quote: Gabe, I sent five pages to a client that, you know, before I would have had to go back and forth with an analyst on over 3 days to create and I made it in 10 minutes myself.

themes.theme: Vertical AI Strategy: Where the Foundation Labs Won't Go

insights.claim: Rogo deliberately builds products 'perpendicular' to what OpenAI and Anthropic will build; for a company on the path from $100B to $1 trillion in revenue, a finance-specific workflow business is comparatively trivial ('stopping on the side of the road to pick up a penny'), leaving deep, messy vertical niches open for specialists.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: The scale mismatch between frontier labs' revenue ambitions and vertical-specific workflow TAM is a durable structural moat argument for vertical AI investors to underwrite.
insights.quote: anthropic would kind of be like, you know, stopping on the side of the road to pick up a penny because they're on the pathway of trying to go from a hundred billion in in revenue to a trillion in revenue.

insights.claim: Rogo targets private markets and dealmakers rather than public equities first because private markets still run on unbuilt 'plumbing' (manual coordination, no standardized data or exchanges), whereas public equities already have automated infrastructure and exchanges, making the wedge opportunity smaller there.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A generalizable heuristic for picking AI verticals: prioritize industries where the underlying transaction/workflow infrastructure is still manual and unbuilt, not just where data happens to be abundant.

insights.claim: Building compliance and audit plumbing for handling material non-public information (MNPI) during live deals is cited as a specific example of the kind of unglamorous regulatory infrastructure that foundation labs will never build but that vertical finance AI companies must own.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Regulatory/compliance plumbing (auditability, MNPI handling) is a concrete, defensible moat category for finance-vertical AI that's easy for investors to check when diligencing competitive risk from foundation labs.

insights.claim: Rogo's CEO believes the ultimate prize in capital markets is not owning the best intelligence but owning the transaction venue, the communication channel between counterparties, the workflows, and the data inputs — he explicitly states OpenAI/Anthropic will never want to build a data-room business.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating fintech/vertical AI moats should weight ownership of the transaction/communication layer (data rooms, exchanges) more heavily than model quality alone when assessing defensibility.
insights.quote: if you actually want to be the exchange for all of high finance and all of capital markets, you not just need to own the intelligence, you need to own the transaction venue, the communication venue, the workflows, and all the data inputs that go into it.

insights.claim: Comparing Claude Code to ChatGPT/Copilot, the underlying models were fairly similar in capability, but Claude's harness and product presentation was far better and drove a large runup in usage — evidence that how a model is packaged and given agency matters as much as raw model quality.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Investors should not assume the 'best model' wins usage share — harness/UX quality can be the deciding competitive variable, which favors application-layer companies with strong product instincts over pure model access.
insights.quote: The models were actually fairly similar, but the harness and the way that it was presented from Claude was far better.

insights.claim: Rogo's CEO offers a three-part framework for evaluating vertical AI application investments: (1) the industry must have enough data/systems complexity to create a real wedge that a generic chatbot can't solve, (2) the founding team needs genuine domain expertise, and (3) the company must be willing to constantly rebuild and cannibalize its own product every ~6 months as models improve.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A ready-made three-factor screening framework investors can apply when diligencing any vertical AI startup pitch, independent of sector.

insights.claim: Rogo's long-term playbook mirrors Bloomberg's historical strategy: offer a bit of data/AI to get in the door, build out full analytics and workflows on top (moving from co-pilot chatbot to full 'autopilot' agents), then own the exchange and communication layer — except the communication channel Rogo needs to build is for agents transacting with each other across firms, not humans.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Signals a specific future product category to watch for: agent-to-agent transaction/negotiation infrastructure across investment firms, effectively an 'exchange' layer for private markets deals.

insights.claim: Rogo intentionally targets large banks (e.g., Bank of America) rather than individual investment funds as its primary customer base, because banks serve as the training/distribution channel for the rest of finance and have vastly more seats than even the ten best single-portfolio-manager public equity funds combined.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A go-to-market lesson for vertical SaaS/AI founders: seat-count and downstream talent-pipeline effects can matter more than average deal size when choosing an initial customer segment.

themes.theme: Business Models & Pricing for AI-era Software

insights.claim: Rogo's CEO distinguishes two emerging AI software business models: classic enterprise per-seat software (Rogo, priced like Bloomberg, FactSet, Capital IQ, Pitchbook, requiring human sales/onboarding) versus 'token consumption' businesses (Cursor, Factory, Claude Code) that can scale usage-based revenue with far fewer people because customers are already comfortable buying pure usage.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A useful lens for valuing AI software companies: usage/token-based businesses can scale revenue near-instantly without headcount, while seat-based enterprise AI businesses in regulated verticals cannot, which should show up in growth-rate and margin expectations.

insights.claim: Anthropic's revenue from selling to Rogo has risen exponentially with no human sales effort required on Anthropic's side, because it is a pure token-consumption model — in contrast to how hard it is for Rogo itself to sell to end financial institutions.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Illustrates the growth-rate gap between infrastructure/model-layer companies (frictionless expansion) and application-layer enterprise sellers in regulated verticals (friction-heavy), relevant to relative growth multiples.

insights.claim: Rogo's CEO predicts every AI software business must pass through two pricing revolutions: first moving from flat/seat pricing to usage-based pricing, then eventually to outcome-based pricing (e.g., charging per good investment idea, per completed SIM, or per LP report), because customers structurally cannot judge whether $100,000 spent on tokens delivered $100,000 of value.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Investors should expect AI software pricing models to keep evolving away from token/seat metrics toward outcome-based pricing; watch for early movers who successfully price on realized value as a signal of pricing power and stickiness.
insights.quote: every business needs to go through two different pricing revolutions. You need to move to some sort of usage based and then you need to move to some sort of outcomebased.

insights.claim: Fixed per-seat pricing creates a structural misalignment risk for AI vendors: if the product gets so good that customers use it far more, the vendor's underlying compute/token costs rise without a corresponding increase in revenue, effectively making heavier usage a worse economic customer.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A margin risk to flag when evaluating seat-priced AI vendors: rising product quality/usage under fixed pricing can compress gross margins rather than expand them, unlike typical SaaS economics.

insights.claim: Because Rogo sells via classic enterprise motions (AE, solutions architect, sales engineer per deal) rather than frictionless API/token consumption, it must build its go-to-market machine roughly five times faster than most enterprise software companies historically have had to, since it cannot rely on a single deal driving 100x usage growth the way token-based competitors can.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Growth-rate comparisons between seat-based enterprise AI vendors and usage-based ones should account for this structural GTM speed constraint rather than treating all 'AI companies' as equally scalable.

insights.claim: Rogo's CEO draws a direct analogy to mortgages: 15-20 years ago nearly all mortgages required an in-person banker conversation, and today 40-50% of mortgages are originated online via platforms like Rocket Mortgage; he expects a similar shift toward self-serve, largely automated capital raising and deal transacting over the next several years.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete historical precedent (mortgage disintermediation, 40-50% online) investors can use to calibrate the pace and ceiling of automation in capital raising and dealmaking.
insights.quote: Now, 40 to 50% of mortgages are just delivered online by platforms like Rocket Mort mortgage.

insights.claim: Rogo's CEO predicts asset pricing and portfolio company sale decisions will compress from months to minutes — e.g., it should eventually take KKR roughly five minutes rather than five months to determine whether to sell a portfolio company to another sponsor — as AI accelerates deal analysis and pricing.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: If private-market deal cycle times compress by orders of magnitude, transaction volumes and market liquidity in private equity secondaries could rise sharply, a thesis worth tracking against actual deal-cycle data over the next few years.
insights.quote: I think it'll be take five minutes for KKR to figure out, can I sell this portfolio company to another sponsor, not 5 months.

insights.claim: JPMorgan has reportedly announced plans to expand M&A coverage into small-and-mid-market businesses it previously couldn't profitably serve because deal fees were too small to justify staffing a full deal team; AI enabling a 'deal team of one' banker changes which parts of the market are economically servable.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Watch large banks' SMB/mid-market M&A coverage expansion as a leading indicator of AI-driven addressable market growth in investment banking, and a potential new revenue line for banks previously priced out of small deals.
insights.quote: if you have a banker that can be a deal team of one, well, maybe you can enter parts of the market that before, you know, just made no sense.

insights.claim: Rogo's CEO identifies two genuine uncertainties for the future of automated private markets: (1) whether regulatory or market forces will push the additional data standardization needed to make historically unstructured private assets tradable, and (2) how much of dealmaking (especially small-business sales involving generational owner handoffs) will always require human trust/relationship rather than fully automatable processes like secondaries, private credit, or GP-LP secondaries.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Frames the two swing factors that will determine how fast and how completely private markets can be automated — both are trackable via regulatory news flow and deal-type mix data.

themes.theme: Trust, Auditability & Agentic Risk in Finance

insights.claim: Concerns about AI 'hallucinations' have largely dropped out of conversation in finance; what now matters more is auditability — users need to see the assumptions and data lineage behind an AI output so they can trust and act on it even when it isn't perfectly accurate, since an answer they can't verify is unusable regardless of accuracy.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Vendors and investors should evaluate finance AI products on transparency/lineage of outputs, not just benchmark accuracy scores, since auditability is what actually drives adoption and trust at institutions.
insights.quote: I think it's actually more important to be auditable than it is to be accurate.

insights.claim: As AI tools shift from 'co-pilot' (information retrieval) to 'autopilot' (agents with execution authority to send emails or make decisions), firms will need full explainability of agent decisions for debugging and regulatory purposes, especially given the prospect that a court could someday make AI-generated investment research and inputs legally discoverable.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Legal discoverability of AI decision trails is an underappreciated compliance risk/requirement; firms and vendors that build full audit lineage now will be better positioned if litigation or regulatory scrutiny of AI-driven decisions increases.
insights.quote: if someday you know some Delaware court judge makes AI inputs and research discoverable you have actually done it all the right way such that you're not intermingling information

themes.theme: Org Design, Talent & Internal AI Culture at Rogo

insights.claim: Rogo records 100% of internal conversations via meeting-transcription tools, feeding a company-wide internal AI system called 'Shrek' that surfaces prior relevant deployments and use cases across the company (e.g., a colleague's conversation from three weeks earlier in APAC) and is explicitly primed with the company's stated goals, values, and north-star metrics.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A transferable enablement tactic for any fast-scaling company: systematically capturing and indexing internal conversations can compound institutional knowledge faster than relying on individual memory or documentation habits.

insights.claim: Rogo publishes a monthly report stack-ranking every employee's AI-tool usage within their division, publicly posting the top five power users and, as a forcing function, giving the bottom-ranked user in each division a printed photo wearing a 'dunce cap' posted around the office.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: An unusually aggressive but concrete example of how AI-native companies are engineering internal incentive structures to force tool adoption — a data point for how far leadership will go to close the individual-to-firm productivity gap.
insights.quote: the bottom user in each division gets a print out with a dun cap and we post it around the office and it's hilarious but people know it's coming

insights.claim: Rogo's CEO believes pure domain expertise and 'GM-like' product intuition are rising in relative value versus raw engineering skill because AI has lowered the bar to writing good code; the company preferentially hires former startup founders (who combine product intuition, engineering chops, and resilience from having built and often failed before).
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A hiring signal for other AI-native companies: as coding gets commoditized by AI, the scarcest and most valuable hire becomes someone with both domain judgment and enough technical fluency to direct AI systems, not pure coding talent.

insights.claim: Rogo has acquired six different fledgling financial-AI startups, largely to bring in former founders with domain expertise and product intuition who had already tried and struggled to solve pieces of the financial-AI problem.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A visible roll-up pattern in the crowded financial-AI startup space: expect continued consolidation as well-capitalized category leaders like Rogo acquihire smaller failed or struggling competitors for talent rather than product.
insights.quote: we've acquired six different kind of fledgling financial AI startups

insights.claim: Citing an anecdote about Max Levchin's firm rebuilding its core ledger technology from scratch every year (to retain engineering talent and prevent the system from becoming ossified), Rogo applies the same practice to its own agentic harness/core system, deliberately treating it as never having reached a local optimum given how fast underlying models change.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A structural practice worth screening for in AI-native companies: willingness to periodically rebuild core infrastructure from scratch (rather than incrementally patch it) may be a leading indicator of long-term competitiveness as models keep improving.

insights.claim: The current model limitation Rogo's CEO most wants solved is 'compaction' — how an AI agent remembers the right things across up to 100 conversations and compresses that memory into a usable token budget while retaining coherence; this problem scales exponentially once agents move from one-to-one use (a single person using ChatGPT/Copilot) to coordinating across many people in shared channels like Slack.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Memory/compaction is flagged as the key unsolved capability bottleneck for multi-agent, multi-user enterprise AI products; a model or infrastructure breakthrough here would be a major unlock worth monitoring across the model labs.

insights.claim: At Rogo's Series A, 40 investors — including Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, and Benchmark, and initially Thrive Capital — passed after extensive engagement (multiple meetings, dinners, IC presentations) before Keith Rabois led the round about a month later.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete data point on how many 'near misses' a category-defining vertical AI company can face before finding its lead investor — useful context for founders and investors calibrating how much early rejection signals about a deal's ultimate quality.
insights.quote: It's so personal cuz at that stage, it has nothing to do with anything but you, right?

insights.claim: Investors who passed on Rogo's Series A cited three reasons in hindsight: underestimating the TAM in finance because Silicon Valley had no pattern-matching intuition for the category (no major venture-backed winners like Ion Group, Bloomberg, S&P, FactSet, Pitchbook, or Morningstar had emerged from VC), the product itself being unreliable at the time ('wrong half the time'), and doubt in the founder's ability to execute given limited visible resilience data points.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Explains a structural blind spot in venture capital toward finance-vertical software (no prior comps), suggesting other 'no obvious venture precedent' categories may be systematically underpriced by pattern-matching investors.

insights.claim: When Keith Rabois challenged the Rogo bet as 'not contrarian' (essentially 'Harvey for finance'), Rogo's CEO argued the real edge was that every other investor who'd met him had passed anyway — implying a bet can be simultaneously consensus-sounding in thesis yet still mispriced because of investor TAM-blindness and unresolved execution doubt.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO) / Keith Rabois
insights.so_what: A reminder that 'obviously good, non-contrarian' theses can still be genuinely mispriced investment opportunities if the market lacks the intuition or conviction to underwrite them at the founder level.
insights.quote: Keith was like Gabe this is kind of this isn't a contrarian bet. It's basically just Harvey for finance. Why would I do it?

insights.claim: As a venture-backed founder, Rogo's CEO frames strategy as deliberately increasing 'both tails of the distribution' — accepting a higher chance of failure (e.g., +30%) if it also raises the odds of becoming a $100 billion company (e.g., +20%), rather than optimizing for the safest, most moderate plan.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: A risk-framing heuristic for evaluating founder decision-making in venture-scale bets: the right strategic move for outlier outcomes should raise both failure risk and outlier-success odds together, not just derisk the median case.
insights.quote: It's fine if it gets 30% more likelihood that I fail if the odds that I become a hundred billion dollar company also increase by 20%.

insights.claim: At a Rogo board meeting, an investor (referred to as Pat) reasoned that because every finance firm will make an AI buying decision within the next 18 months regardless, the only strategy that matters is blitzing the market as fast as possible to make sure Rogo is present for that decision — and judged Rogo's next-year hiring/commercial/product plan not aggressive enough by that logic.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO), referencing board input
insights.so_what: A specific strategic logic for AI-vertical land-grabs: if customer AI adoption within a fixed near-term window (e.g., 18 months) is inevitable regardless of vendor quality, speed of market presence becomes the dominant strategic variable over incremental plan quality.

insights.claim: Rogo's CEO argues that in this AI cycle, the winning company in each vertical will become a 'black hole' for talent, capital, and brand because the execution bar for competing has risen sharply; companies that fail to attract that gravity are at high risk of being displaced either by a foundation lab or by a better-resourced competitor.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: Supports a power-law, winner-take-most framework for vertical AI investing: capital should concentrate in the emerging category leader per vertical rather than spreading bets evenly, since second-place finishers face disproportionate risk.
insights.quote: if you can't figure out what is the strategy to become a black hole for talent and capital as quickly as possible, I do think you are far more at risk at being roadkill of a lab or a company that can.

insights.claim: As an early example of a prescient 'AI-native' leader, a co-founder at an investment bank (referred to in the conversation as John Mumazi) pushed years ago to build digital clones of the bank's best bankers — replicating their voice, judgment, and relationships so any junior banker could instantly leverage that expertise on calls — an idea that sounded far-fetched at the time but now looks prescient.
insights.speaker: Gabe (Rogo CEO)
insights.so_what: An early real-world example of the 'digital clone of top talent' pattern that Rogo's CEO expects will spread across investment banks — worth watching which banks operationalize this first as a competitive signal.
